title: 05 — Data Modeling
html:
05 — Data Modeling

The one idea: a data model is a set of promises about what one row means. Operational models promise that every fact is stored once so it can be updated safely; analytical models promise that every question can be answered with few joins and consistent definitions. Pick the promise that matches the workload, then state the grain out loud.

1. Normalisation vs denormalisation

Normalisation (1NF → 2NF → 3NF) splits data so each fact lives in exactly one place:

  • 1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups (no phone1, phone2, phone3 columns).
  • 2NF: every non-key column depends on the whole key (no attributes that depend on only part of a composite key).
  • 3NF: non-key columns depend only on the key, not on other non-key columns (no zip_code → city inside the customer table).

Denormalisation deliberately re-introduces redundancy so reads need fewer joins.

Normalised (3NF) Denormalised (dimensional / wide)
Optimised for Writes, integrity Reads, aggregation
Update anomalies Avoided Possible; handled by the pipeline, not users
Joins per query Many Few
Understandable by analysts Harder Easier
Typical home OLTP, silver-layer entity tables, Inmon enterprise layer Gold marts, BI models

In a lakehouse, storage is cheap and joins across billions of rows are expensive, so the gold layer is almost always denormalised. Silver often stays closer to the source's normalised shape, cleaned and conformed.

2. Kimball dimensional modelling

Kimball's method is a four-step design process:

  1. Choose the business process — e.g. retail sales, order fulfilment, subscription billing. Model processes, not departments.
  2. Declare the grain — exactly what one fact row represents: "one row per order line", "one row per account per day".
  3. Identify the dimensions — the who/what/where/when/how context that is true at that grain.
  4. Identify the facts — the numeric measurements true at that grain.

Declaring the grain first is the single most important habit. Most modelling bugs are grain bugs: mixing order-level shipping cost into an order-line fact and then summing it (double counting), or joining a daily snapshot to a transaction fact.

Facts and dimensions

Fact table Dimension table
Contains Measures (amount, quantity, duration) + foreign keys Descriptive attributes (name, category, region)
Row count Very large (millions to billions) Small to medium
Shape Narrow and deep Wide and shallow
Changes Mostly inserts Attributes change slowly over time
Keys Composite of dimension surrogate keys (+ degenerate dimensions) Surrogate key + natural key

Measure additivity

Type Can be summed across... Example
Additive All dimensions Sales amount, quantity
Semi-additive Some dimensions, not time Account balance, inventory level (sum across accounts, but average or take last over days)
Non-additive None Ratios, percentages, unit price (store numerator and denominator instead)

Star vs snowflake

---
title: Star schema for retail sales
---
erDiagram
    FACT_SALES }o--|| DIM_DATE : "date_key"
    FACT_SALES }o--|| DIM_PRODUCT : "product_key"
    FACT_SALES }o--|| DIM_STORE : "store_key"
    FACT_SALES }o--|| DIM_CUSTOMER : "customer_key"
    FACT_SALES {
        int date_key
        int product_key
        int store_key
        int customer_key
        string order_number
        int quantity
        decimal net_amount
    }
    DIM_PRODUCT {
        int product_key
        string product_code
        string product_name
        string category
        string department
    }
    DIM_CUSTOMER {
        int customer_key
        string customer_id
        string name
        string segment
        date valid_from
        date valid_to
        boolean is_current
    }
Star Snowflake
Dimensions Denormalised (category and department inside dim_product) Normalised into sub-tables (dim_product → dim_category → dim_department)
Joins One hop from fact to each dimension Chains of joins
Storage Slightly more Slightly less
Query simplicity and speed Better Worse
Recommendation Default Only when a sub-dimension is large, shared and independently maintained

Conformed dimensions

A conformed dimension has the same keys, attribute names and meanings in every fact table that uses it. With one conformed dim_customer, you can put sales, support tickets and returns side by side in one report ("drill across"). Without it, each mart invents its own customer and the numbers never reconcile. The bus matrix — business processes as rows, dimensions as columns, ticks where they meet — is the planning tool for this.

Special dimension patterns

Pattern What it is
Degenerate dimension A dimension value with no table, stored on the fact (order number, invoice number)
Junk dimension Combines several low-cardinality flags (is_gift, payment_type, channel) into one small dimension to keep the fact narrow
Role-playing dimension One dimension used several times with different meanings (dim_date as order date, ship date, delivery date)
Date dimension A pre-built calendar table with fiscal periods, holidays, weekday flags; every warehouse has one
Bridge table Resolves many-to-many relationships (an account with several holders)
Inferred member Placeholder dimension row for a late-arriving dimension, updated when real data arrives

3. Fact table types

Type Grain Updated? Example Typical measures
Transaction One row per event No, insert-only fact_payment: one row per payment Amount, quantity
Periodic snapshot One row per entity per period No, new rows each period fact_account_balance_daily Balance, open positions (semi-additive)
Accumulating snapshot One row per process instance Yes, as milestones complete fact_order_fulfilment with ordered/picked/shipped/delivered dates Lags between milestones, counts
Factless One row per occurrence or coverage No fact_class_attendance, fact_promotion_coverage None (counting rows is the measure)

Accumulating snapshots are the only fact type that is regularly updated, which on a lakehouse means MERGE. Transaction and periodic snapshot facts are append or partition-overwrite.

4. Slowly changing dimensions

Dimension attributes change: customers move, products are recategorised. The SCD type decides whether history is kept and how.

Starting point for all examples — customer C100 lives in Leeds:

customer_key customer_id name city
1 C100 Asha Leeds

On 2026-06-01, she moves to Bristol.

Type 0 — retain original

The value never changes after first load. Used for attributes that are defined as fixed ("original acquisition channel", "date of birth as first recorded").

customer_key customer_id name original_city
1 C100 Asha Leeds

Type 1 — overwrite

customer_key customer_id name city
1 C100 Asha Bristol

No history. Last year's sales now appear under Bristol. Right for corrections (typo fixes) and attributes where history does not matter.

Type 2 — add a new row

customer_key customer_id name city valid_from valid_to is_current
1 C100 Asha Leeds 2023-02-10 2026-06-01 false
2 C100 Asha Bristol 2026-06-01 9999-12-31 true

Full history. Facts loaded before the move keep customer_key = 1 (Leeds); new facts get customer_key = 2. This is the workhorse of dimensional history. Conventions to agree on: whether valid_to is exclusive (as here) or inclusive, and whether open rows use 9999-12-31 or NULL.

Type 3 — add a column

customer_key customer_id name current_city previous_city
1 C100 Asha Bristol Leeds

Limited history (one prior value). Useful for "before/after a reorganisation" reporting, e.g. old and new sales territories side by side.

Type 4 — history table (or mini-dimension)

Two common interpretations exist, so agree which one your team means.

History-table interpretation: the main dimension holds only current values; every version goes to a separate history table.

dim_customer (current):

customer_key customer_id name city
1 C100 Asha Bristol

dim_customer_history:

customer_id city valid_from valid_to
C100 Leeds 2023-02-10 2026-06-01
C100 Bristol 2026-06-01 9999-12-31

Kimball interpretation (mini-dimension): rapidly changing attributes (age band, credit score band) are split out into their own small dimension, referenced directly from the fact, so the main dimension does not explode with type 2 rows.

Type 6 — hybrid (1 + 2 + 3)

Type 2 rows for history, plus a current_city column that is overwritten (type 1) on every row for that customer.

customer_key customer_id name historical_city current_city valid_from valid_to is_current
1 C100 Asha Leeds Bristol 2023-02-10 2026-06-01 false
2 C100 Asha Bristol Bristol 2026-06-01 9999-12-31 true

Now a report can group last year's sales by historical city (as it was when sold) or by current city (restated) without extra joins.

Choosing

Need Type
Never changes by definition 0
Only the latest value matters, or fixing errors 1
Report "as it was at the time" 2
Compare to exactly one previous value 3
Many fast-changing attributes bloating a type 2 dimension 4 (mini-dimension)
Both "as was" and "as is" reporting 6

A full SCD2 MERGE implementation in SQL and PySpark is in Delta Lake. Databricks' declarative pipelines also offer a built-in way to apply CDC as SCD1 or SCD2 (APPLY CHANGES / AUTO CDC), covered in chapter 07.

5. Data Vault 2.0

Data Vault is designed for integrating many source systems with full auditability, and for loading in parallel without cross-table dependencies. It is an integration-layer model, not something analysts query directly; you build star schemas (information marts) on top.

---
title: Data Vault — hubs, links and satellites
---
flowchart LR
    HC["HUB_CUSTOMER<br/>customer_hk, customer_id,<br/>load_ts, record_source"]
    HO["HUB_ORDER<br/>order_hk, order_number,<br/>load_ts, record_source"]
    L["LINK_CUSTOMER_ORDER<br/>link_hk, customer_hk, order_hk,<br/>load_ts, record_source"]
    SC["SAT_CUSTOMER_DETAILS<br/>customer_hk, load_ts, hash_diff,<br/>name, email, city"]
    SO["SAT_ORDER_STATUS<br/>order_hk, load_ts, hash_diff,<br/>status, amount"]
    HC --- L
    HO --- L
    HC --- SC
    HO --- SO
Component Holds Changes
Hub Unique business keys of a core concept + hash key + load timestamp + record source Insert-only
Link Relationships between hubs (by hash keys) Insert-only
Satellite Descriptive attributes and their history for a hub or link, with a hash_diff to detect changes Insert-only (a new row when hash_diff changes)

Hash keys (e.g. SHA-256 or MD5 of the normalised business key) let hubs, links and satellites be loaded in parallel, since no load needs to look up a sequence-generated key from another table.

Strengths Weaknesses
Absorbs new sources and schema changes by adding satellites, not remodelling Many tables and joins; not query-friendly
Full audit trail: everything is insert-only with source and load time Needs automation (code generation) to be practical
Parallel loading Business rules are deferred, so you still need marts on top

Use it when you integrate many volatile sources and auditability is a hard requirement (regulated industries). For most lakehouse teams with a handful of sources, a medallion architecture with dimensional gold models is simpler.

6. One Big Table (OBT)

OBT denormalises everything into one very wide table per business process: the fact and every dimension attribute, pre-joined.

Pros Cons
Zero joins for consumers, simple for BI and ad-hoc SQL Dimension changes (type 1) require rewriting huge volumes
Columnar storage makes unused columns nearly free to store and skip Metric logic can still diverge without a semantic layer
Works well with modern engines and clustering Duplicated attributes across several OBTs drift apart

A pragmatic combination: keep a proper star schema as the source of truth in gold, and build OBT views or tables from it for specific dashboards that need speed and simplicity.

7. Medallion architecture

---
title: Medallion architecture — bronze, silver, gold
---
flowchart LR
    S1["Source systems<br/>DBs, APIs, events, files"] --> B["Bronze<br/>raw, append-only,<br/>full fidelity"]
    B --> SV["Silver<br/>cleaned, typed, deduplicated,<br/>conformed entities"]
    SV --> G1["Gold<br/>star schemas and marts"]
    SV --> G2["Gold<br/>aggregates and KPIs"]
    SV --> G3["Gold<br/>ML feature tables"]
    B -.->|"replay if silver logic changes"| SV
Layer What belongs here What does not Write pattern Consumers
Bronze Data as received: raw payload (string/VARIANT or parsed with a permissive schema), source file name, ingestion timestamp, source system Business logic, filtering, deduplication Append-only Data engineers only
Silver Typed columns, standardised formats (dates, currencies, codes), deduplication, basic quality rules applied (quarantine the rest), CDC applied into current-state or SCD2 entity tables, conformed keys Report-specific aggregates, department-specific logic Merge / upsert, append for events Data engineers, data scientists, analytics engineers
Gold Facts and dimensions, aggregates, KPI tables, feature tables, data products for specific consumers Raw or uncleaned data Overwrite by partition, merge, materialized views Analysts, BI, applications, ML

Practical guidance:

  • Bronze is your insurance policy. If silver logic is wrong, you rebuild silver from bronze. Keep bronze long enough to allow that (with retention and PII rules applied).
  • Silver is where most of the engineering happens. It should be source-aligned but business-meaningful: silver.customers, not silver.crm_tbl_cust_v2.
  • Gold is consumer-aligned. It is fine to have several gold tables derived from the same silver data for different use cases.
  • The three layers are a convention, not a law. Some teams add a landing zone before bronze or split gold into "gold" and "platinum"/semantic. What matters is that each layer has a clear contract.
  • Medallion describes quality levels, not modelling style. You still choose Kimball, Data Vault or OBT for what goes inside silver and gold.

Azure / .NET mapping

Concept Where it shows up
Normalised OLTP model Your EF Core entities in Azure SQL — a 3NF source for silver
Star schema serving Power BI semantic models work best with a star schema; import or DirectQuery against Databricks SQL
Medallion layers Commonly one Unity Catalog catalog per environment with bronze, silver, gold schemas, or one catalog per layer
Data Vault automation Code-generation tools or dbt packages run on Databricks or Synapse

Power BI's own modelling guidance strongly favours star schemas; a snowflaked or OBT-only model tends to produce slower and more confusing reports.

Review checklist

  • For every fact table I design, I can state its grain in one sentence.
  • I can distinguish additive, semi-additive and non-additive measures.
  • I can explain star vs snowflake and why star is the default.
  • I know why conformed dimensions matter for drill-across reporting.
  • I can name the four fact table types and which one gets updated.
  • I can draw before/after tables for SCD types 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6.
  • I can explain hubs, links and satellites and when Data Vault is worth it.
  • I know what belongs in bronze, silver and gold, and that medallion is about quality levels, not modelling style.
